UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
Pre-filed Comments of Maria Gulluni, ISO New England Inc. 
Panel 1: PJM Governance Mechanics, Board Authority, States’ Role, Filing Rights,  
and Document Architecture 
 
I respectfully submit these comments in advance of the technical conference convened by 
the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (Commission) on July 23, 2026 to discuss the 
governance and stakeholder processes of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM).  I appreciate the 
invitation to join you on Panel 1. 
New England, of course, is a smaller and more defined region than PJM’s control area, 
and its states’ energy policies and regulatory structure are generally more aligned than in PJM 
(although not perfectly so).  Given these characteristics, ISO New England Inc. (ISO-NE) may 
have fewer challenges than PJM in working with its states and market participants on regional 
energy issues.  Nonetheless, to the extent it is helpful, I will describe our governance structure in 
this document. 
I outline below the governance mechanics cited in the description of the first panel, 
including Board authority, the states’ role, filing rights, and document architecture.  I will focus 
on the ways, to my knowledge, that ISO-NE’s mechanics differ from that of PJM.1   
Document Architecture.  At the highest level, ISO-NE’s governing documents fall into 
three categories:  corporate; terms and conditions of service; and market participants and states.  
All of these documents are referenced throughout these comments.   
On the corporate side, ISO-NE has a Certificate of Incorporation and By-Laws, both of 
which outline its internal governance.2  In the second category, ISO-NE’s terms and conditions of 
market and transmission service are outlined in:  the Transmission Operating Agreement, which 
describes the split of responsibilities between ISO-NE and the region’s transmission owners for

differences, are there lessons from other regional transmission organization/independent system operator (RTO/ISO) 
governance structures that PJM could reasonably adopt to improve its responsiveness to the region’s operational and 
market challenges?”

managing the transmission system, and is the vehicle through which ISO-NE was assigned the 
rights to make filings with the Commission pursuant to Section 205 of the Federal Power Act (as 
discussed below);3 and ISO-NE’s single Tariff, which includes sections on the markets, open 
transmission access, and ISO-NE’s rate recovery.4   
Finally, regarding market participants and states, the relevant documents describe their 
organizations, as well as ISO-NE’s interactions with those organizations.5  Notably, as set forth 
in the Participants Agreement, New England’s market participants formed the New England 
Power Pool (NEPOOL) in 1971.  NEPOOL has its own governance structure and counsel.  The 
states’ representative organizations are described in the next section.   
States’ Role.  The New England states are represented by two organizations.  The New 
England Conference of Public Utilities Commissioners (NECPUC) “provides regional regulatory 
assistance” to New England’s public utilities commissions on topics including water, gas, 
electricity, and telecommunications.6  New England’s Regional State Committee, the New 
England States Committee on Electricity (NESCOE), was formed later than NECPUC and is 
more narrowly focused on electricity issues.7  NESCOE is directed by a committee composed of 
representatives appointed by each of the six New England governors, in his or her discretion; in 
practice, these appointees generally include energy policy officials as well as public utilities 
commissioners.8 
NESCOE is funded through a rate in ISO-NE’s Tariff that is paid by Regional Network 
Load.9  The rate is based on NESCOE’s annually-filed budget that is approved by the

Commission.10  For fiscal year 2026, NESCOE’s total budget is $2,731,108, largely for staff 
compensation and consulting services for economic, engineering and financial analysis.11   
Given its resourcing, NESCOE is able to work through the market participant process as 
a fully committed and informed partner on markets and transmission initiatives.  In fact, 
NESCOE has committed to work within that process to present policy proposals for stakeholder 
consideration, and is required to collaborate with stakeholders to reach negotiated solutions 
where possible.12   
NESCOE has committed to “make every effort to avoid duplication of efforts or 
conflicting policy positions” with NECPUC.13  NESCOE achieves this objective by meeting 
jointly with NECPUC, ISO-NE and stakeholders, and formally coordinating with NECPUC.  
While this coordination is required at least once annually to allocate lead responsibility for 
regional electric policy issues to “avoid conflicting recommendations and to make efficient use 
of available staff,”14 in practice it occurs much more frequently. 
ISO-NE also works with the states’ consumer advocates through the NEPOOL process, as 
many consumer advocates are members of NEPOOL’s end user sector.  Consumers and 
consumer advocates also interact with ISO-NE through the Consumer Liaison Group, which was 
formed as part of the region’s compliance with the Commission’s Order No. 719.15   
Board Authority.  Unlike PJM, ISO-NE is a non-stock, not-for-profit corporation 
organized pursuant to Delaware law.  Its Board of Directors is composed of nine independent 
members and the CEO, who is a non-voting member.  The Board of Directors also serves as the 
members of the Company, filling the role that shareholders play in a for-profit company.16  The 
Board does much of its work through its standing committees, which include Audit and Finance; 
Compensation and Human Resources; Nominating and Governance; Information Technology 
and Cyber Security; Markets; and System Planning and Reliability.17 
The Board’s role is to provide direction on the management of the Company;18 as such, it 
is an oversight body.  While the Board and its relevant committees are certainly made aware of

major filings, including the underlying designs and stakeholder and state positions, the Board 
does not propose, review or vote on filings in the manner of PJM’s Board of Managers.19  
New members of the Board are nominated through a process that includes representatives 
of the Board, NEPOOL members, and the states, working together as part of a Joint Nominating 
Committee.  The Committee seeks to reach consensus on new candidates.20  Following 
nomination by the Committee, NEPOOL votes on the slate, with a vote of 70% required to 
endorse the slate.21  Finally, the Board completes the process with a vote to elect.22 
Board members must have a cross-section of skills, such as Commission electric 
regulatory affairs, energy industry management, corporate finance, bulk power systems, power 
pool operations, public policy, distributed generation or demand response technologies, 
renewable energy, consumer advocacy, environmental affairs, business management and 
information technologies.  At least three directors must have electric industry experience, and 
preference is given to New Englanders.23  Directors are subject to term limits and an age limit to 
facilitate turnover.24  
 The Board interacts regularly with NEPOOL and the states (both NECPUC and 
NESCOE).  Per the Participants Agreement, Board members are invited to NEPOOL meetings, 
which they regularly attend, and additionally meet with NEPOOL at least twice per year.25  
These twice-yearly meetings occur between members of the Board and the individual sectors of 
NEPOOL, which are Transmission, Generation, Suppliers, Publicly-Owned Entities, Alternative 
Resources, and End Users.26 
By practice, the Board also meets with representatives of both NECPUC and NESCOE 
twice per year, and has developed a “state liaison” program.  Per that program, the Board assigns 
two directors to each New England state public utilities commission.  These liaisons are available 
for the commissions to contact at any time, and the liaisons meet with their assigned 
commissions at least annually.  Each state commission usually invites the state’s governor-
appointed NESCOE manager to these meetings. 
Filing Rights.  As set out in ISO-NE’s agreement with the region’s transmission owners, 
ISO-NE has the filing rights under Section 205 of the Federal Power Act with respect to both the 
markets and the non-rate terms and conditions of transmission service.  The transmission owners

retain their rights to set revenue requirements for transmission facilities and establish terms and

ISO-NE has contractually shared its Section 205 rights with NEPOOL via a “jump ball;” 
pursuant to the relevant provision of the Participants Agreement, if NEPOOL approves an 
alternative to an ISO-NE market rule proposal, ISO-NE must file that alternative with the 
Commission pursuant to Section 205 on equal footing with ISO-NE’s own proposal.28  
This “jump ball” right extends to a proposal made by NESCOE.  As noted above, 
NESCOE has committed to work within the participant process and present its policy proposals 
through that process.29  If NEPOOL supports an alternative market rule change proposed by 
NESCOE, the “jump ball” provision applies to that proposal.30  The states have other rights 
pursuant to the Tariff, as well, including decision-making on certain transmission planning 
projects through the Longer-Term Transmission Planning process.31  States can also provide 
scenarios to analyze through ISO-NE’s economic studies32 and Probabilistic Energy Adequacy 
Tool.  
The transmission owners also granted NESCOE a “jump ball” regarding proposals for the 
allocation of the costs of generation and transmission interconnection upgrades.  Pursuant to that 
provision of the Transmission Operating Agreement, if NESCOE opposes the transmission 
owners’ cost allocation proposal for interconnection costs, NESCOE may provide the 
transmission owners with an alternative proposal that must be included in the transmission 
owners’ filing with the Commission on equal footing.33
